title: the third

segments.voice: Yesterday: vand chakna, share, then eat. Your line was the second pillar. What did you share before you enjoyed it? Day eleven.

Picture a stool with two legs. You can balance on it for a moment if you're careful, but the second you lean the wrong way, down you go. Now add a third leg, and suddenly you can sit on it all day. For two days we've been building something like that stool. Honest work. Sharing what you earn. Both good, both solid. But a person could do both and still feel hollow: busy and generous and running on empty, forgetting what any of it is for. The Gurus added a third leg, and in a way it holds the other two up. Today, the last of the three pillars.
screen: `A STOOL WITH TWO LEGS.` → `BUSY, GENEROUS, AND EMPTY.` → `THE THIRD LEG.`

segments.voice: Naam japna. Naam, the name, the word you met on day five: not just a label but the whole presence of God, the truth running through everything. Japna means to repeat, to recite, to keep saying. So: keep the name. Remember God, again and again, all through the day. If this sounds familiar, it should. On day seven you learned simran, remembrance, Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath. Naam japna is the same heart, set in its place as a pillar of the whole life. It can be quiet, a word on the breath. It can be loud, a room full of people singing the scripture together to drums and harmonium. It can be reading, or listening, or simply catching yourself in the middle of a busy afternoon and remembering what's real. Here's why the Gurus put it with work and sharing. Without it, honest work can turn into pride: look how hard I work. Sharing can turn into a show: look how much I give. Remembering the name keeps both humble, because it reminds you where the strength to work and the things you share came from in the first place. And it runs the other way too. Remembering God without working honestly or sharing would float off into the clouds. The Sikh life keeps all three on the ground, together. Work with your hands. Share with your hands. Remember with your whole self. Earn it clean, share it first, and keep the name. That's the stool. Three legs, and a person can sit steady on it for a lifetime.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME. JAPNA — TO REPEAT.` · `SIMRAN, SET AS A PILLAR.` · `IT KEEPS WORK AND GIVING HUMBLE.` · `WORK, SHARE, REMEMBER, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE THREE PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and feel what you're sitting on, the chair, the floor, the bed. Notice how it holds you up without you thinking about it. Now breathe slowly. If you'd like, let the name ride on the breath: Wahe in, guru out. If that word isn't yours, let each breath carry one thing you want to remember is real. Just keep coming back to it. The bell holds the time.
Naam japna. Keeping the name: remembering God again and again, through the day. The third pillar, beside honest work and sharing. Eleventh word.
Your line: the three pillars. Today, see if you can touch all three before bed: one honest piece of work, one thing shared, one moment of remembering. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IT IS AND ISN'T.`

howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam japna by repeating Waheguru, reciting daily prayers and singing the scripture together in kirtan; with honest work and sharing it forms the three pillars of Sikh life.

myth: naam japna can only be done silently
it can be a word on the breath, reading, listening, or a room singing together.
naam japna and simran share the same heart
both mean remembering God and the name, again and again.
the third pillar keeps work and giving humble
remembering the name reminds you where the strength to work and share came from.

fork.setup: you work honestly and share generously, but you feel hollow and proud at the same time. what's missing?
fork.reveal: the third pillar, naam japna, keeps the other two humble. three legs, and the stool stands.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: naam (the name) + japna (to repeat, recite).

trapdoor: what you thought: saying God's name a lot.
what it means: keeping the name: remembering God through the day, the pillar that holds work and sharing together.
what a scholar hears: japna is related to jap, repetition, the same root as the title Japji. naam in Sikh usage is the divine presence itself, not only a word.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, passim (naam, and remembering the name)
Sikh teaching of the three pillars: naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna

notes: The relationship between naam japna and simran is described as 'the same heart'; some teachers distinguish them. Confirm.
Trapdoor links japna to jap and the title Japji (the Japji is taught on day 21); confirm the etymological link.
The stool image is the script's own illustration, not a traditional one.
